title: Mock 3 · Balanced Lap
blurb: Even spread across all chapters, with a CPPI rebalancing caselet.

questions.q: If the real risk-free rate is 3% and expected inflation is 5%, the nominal risk-free rate as computed in the workbook is:
questions.explanation: NRR = [(1 + real) x (1 + inflation)] - 1 = 1.0815 - 1 = 8.15% (Section 1.4.1).
hints: Simple addition ignores the cross term.

questions.q: A company has a market capitalisation of ₹800 crore, market value of debt of ₹300 crore and excess cash of ₹100 crore. Its enterprise value is:
questions.explanation: EV = market cap of equity + market value of debt - excess cash (Section 3.4).

questions.q: Which bond has a Macaulay duration exactly equal to its remaining maturity?
options: A high-coupon bond trading at a premium
questions.explanation: Section 4.5.2.1: only a zero-coupon bond has duration equal to its remaining maturity.
hints: A floater's duration is only to the next reset.

questions.q: The buyer of an option contract has:
options: The right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying, for which a premium is paid
An obligation to buy the underlying at expiry
An obligation to pay margin to the option writer daily
The right to receive a premium from the seller
questions.explanation: Options give the buyer a right, not an obligation; the buyer pays a premium to the seller (Chapter 5).
hints: Buyers pay premium margin; the seller faces margin calls.

questions.q: For a mutual fund scheme that has existed for more than three years, performance advertisements must show CAGR for:
options: 1 year, 3 years, 5 years and since inception, with benchmark returns
questions.explanation: Section 6.11: CAGR for 1, 3, 5 years and since inception with benchmark; also point-to-point value of ₹10,000.
hints: That is for liquid and money market schemes.

questions.q: A portfolio manager must keep the funds of all clients in a separate account maintained with:
questions.explanation: Section 7.5: funds of all clients in a separate account maintained in a Scheduled Commercial Bank.
hints: Must be a Scheduled Commercial Bank (Second Schedule to RBI Act).
Funds are kept in a bank account, not custodian's own.

questions.q: When a portfolio manager aggregates purchases for several clients for economies of scale, the securities must be allocated:
options: Pro rata, at the weighted average price of the day's transactions, with no open position left
First to the largest client at the lowest price
At the manager's discretion at any price
Equally among all clients regardless of portfolio size
questions.explanation: Section 7.6.3 (Don'ts, point 11): inter se allocation on a pro rata basis at the weighted average price of the day; no open positions.
hints: Allocation must be pro rata at weighted average price.
Must be pro rata, not equal.

questions.q: Operating expenses charged by a portfolio manager, excluding brokerage and over and above the PMS fees, cannot exceed:
options: 1% per annum of the closing AUM
0.50% per annum of the client's average daily AUM
0.25% per quarter of the opening AUM
questions.explanation: SEBI circular of 13 February 2020: operating expenses excluding brokerage shall not exceed 0.50% p.a. of average daily AUM.

questions.q: Under SEBI's direct onboarding requirement for PMS, when a client is onboarded directly:
options: A reduced upfront fee may be charged
A distribution fee is still payable to APMI
The minimum investment drops to ₹25 lakh
No charges except statutory charges can be levied
questions.explanation: Section 8.4: at the time of direct onboarding no charges except statutory charges shall be levied (not applicable to co-investment PMS).
hints: Upfront fees are not allowed at all.

questions.q: In the life-cycle of investing, the phase in which living expenses are met from accumulated assets rather than earned income is the:
questions.explanation: Section 9.3.9: in the spending phase living expenses are covered from investments; focus is stability.

questions.q: Gains on transfer of listed equity shares are treated as long-term capital gains when the shares are held for:
questions.explanation: Section 10.2.1: listed securities, equity MF units, UTI units and zero-coupon bonds: long term if held more than 12 months.
hints: Applies to unlisted shares and other securities.

questions.q: Under the SEBI insider trading code for intermediaries, pre-cleared trades must be executed within:
questions.explanation: Section 11.2: the timeframe for executing pre-cleared trades shall not be more than seven trading days.
hints: 6 months is the minimum contra-trade restriction.
Correct; otherwise fresh pre-clearance is needed.

questions.q: Which of the following is deemed a fraudulent or unfair trade practice under SEBI PFUTP Regulations, 2003?
options: A market participant trading on behalf of a client without the client's knowledge or instructions
Placing a limit order on a stock exchange
Publishing audited financial results on time
Hedging a portfolio with index futures
questions.explanation: Section 11.3: transactions on behalf of a client without knowledge/instructions, or misusing client funds held in fiduciary capacity, are fraudulent.

questions.q: In a price-weighted index, one stock undergoes a 2-for-1 split. What happens?
options: The divisor stays the same; the index falls
The index value stays the same; the divisor is reduced
Both index and divisor stay the same
questions.explanation: Illustration 12.1: after a split, the divisor is adjusted (e.g. 3.7 to 3.2) so the index level is unchanged.
hints: That would create an artificial fall.
Correct: divisor adjusted to keep the level.
The sum of prices changes, so the divisor must change.

questions.q: Small firms consistently earning higher risk-adjusted returns than large firms is called the:
questions.explanation: Section 13.4.2: firm size anomaly; small cap portfolios are a direct outcome.
hints: Not one of the EMH anomalies listed in Ch 13.

questions.q: A stock may return 30%, 12% or -5% with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3. Its expected return is:
questions.explanation: Ex-ante expected return = Σ pᵢRᵢ = 10.5% (Section 15.4).
hints: Simple average of the three outcomes is 12.33%; this is also wrong.

questions.q: Using CAPM, what is the required return on a stock with a beta of 1.4 if the risk-free rate is 7% and the market risk premium is 8%?
Value at Risk (VaR) is best described as:
options: The worst possible loss in any scenario
The average loss on all losing days
The estimated maximum loss over a given period at a given confidence level under normal market conditions
The probability that the portfolio loses money
questions.explanation: Section 17.4.2: VaR = maximum potential loss over a period, with a given probability, under particular (normal) market conditions.
hints: VaR does not capture worst-case tail losses.
That is closer to expected shortfall, not VaR.
VaR is an amount, not a probability.

questions.q: A manager making forecasts that turn out right 60 times out of 80 has an Information Coefficient of:
questions.explanation: IC = 2 x (right predictions/total predictions) - 1 = 2 x 0.75 - 1 = 0.5 (Section 18.3.1).
hints: That is the hit rate, not IC.

questions.q: Excluding companies involved in alcohol, tobacco, gambling and weapons from an SRI portfolio is called:
questions.explanation: Section 18.9.1: negative screening excludes restricted businesses.
hints: Positive screening ranks and picks high ESG scorers.
Picks the highest rated in each sector.
Not an SRI screening approach in the workbook.

questions.q: An investor with a liability due in 8 years wants to immunize perfectly using a single instrument. The theoretically best choice is:
options: A floating rate bond maturing in 8 years
A zero-coupon bond maturing in 8 years
A portfolio of 1-year T-bills rolled over
questions.explanation: Section 19.2.3: a zero-coupon bond with matching maturity is theoretically the best portfolio to immunize against interest rate risk.
hints: Floater duration is only to the next reset.
Correct: no reinvestment risk; duration equals maturity.
Exposes the investor to reinvestment risk.

questions.q: A portfolio returns 16% with a standard deviation of 20% when the risk-free rate is 6%. Its Sharpe ratio is:
questions.explanation: Sharpe = (Rp - Rf)/σp = 10/20 = 0.5.

questions.q: How much should initially be invested in the risky asset?
questions.explanation: CPPI: risky exposure = m x (portfolio value - floor) = 3 x 40 = ₹120 lakh.
hints: That is the cushion, not the exposure.
questions.case: A family office gives a portfolio manager ₹200 lakh with an instruction that the portfolio must not fall below a floor of ₹160 lakh. The manager runs a CPPI strategy with a multiplier of 3, investing the rest in a risk-free asset whose value can be assumed constant over the short period considered. Ignore transaction costs and taxes.

questions.q: How much goes into the risk-free asset at the start?
questions.explanation: Risk-free allocation = total portfolio - risky exposure = 200 - 120 = ₹80 lakh.
questions.case: A family office gives a portfolio manager ₹200 lakh with an instruction that the portfolio must not fall below a floor of ₹160 lakh. The manager runs a CPPI strategy with a multiplier of 3, investing the rest in a risk-free asset whose value can be assumed constant over the short period considered. Ignore transaction costs and taxes.

questions.q: Soon after, the risky asset falls by 10%. To restore the CPPI rule, the manager should:
options: Buy ₹12 lakh more of the risky asset
Sell ₹12 lakh of the risky asset
Do nothing until the floor is hit
Sell ₹24 lakh of the risky asset
questions.explanation: Risky asset 120 → 108; portfolio = 108 + 80 = 188; cushion = 28; required exposure = 3 x 28 = 84; sell 24 lakh.
hints: CPPI reduces exposure after a fall.
Only removes the loss, not the rule-based amount.
CPPI rebalances as the cushion changes.
Risky = 108, portfolio = 188, new exposure = 3 x 28 = 84; sell 108 - 84 = 24.
